01 — About

The Vision

Mission

Nullfield is Gaurang's personal technology brand built around a single belief: the most futuristic interfaces from science fiction can be built today, with accessible hardware and open-source software.

The mission is to close the gap between imagination and reality — one project at a time. Starting with holographic displays, gesture recognition, and interactive 3D environments that anyone can build from their bedroom.

Core Goal

Build a Pepper's Ghost holographic pyramid that displays 4 interactive 3D wireframe models, navigated entirely through mid-air hand gestures — no touching required.

Architecture

Three independent "brains" — a gesture sensor (Arduino), a renderer (Processing), and a passive optical system (the acrylic pyramid) — each testable in isolation.

02 — Project

How It Works

The system chains three independent components: a gesture sensor translates hand movements into serial commands, a Processing sketch renders 3D models in a 4-panel layout in real time, and the acrylic pyramid reflects the panels into a single floating holographic image.

Arduino UnoProcessing 4APDS-9960Pepper's GhostClear Acrylic 2mmUSB SerialJavaC++
01
Sense
APDS-9960 detects hand swipe direction. Arduino sends a single character over USB serial with an 800ms cooldown to prevent misfires.
02
Parse
Processing listens on the serial port. On newline, it reads the command and instantly updates the animation state object.
03
Render
Four rotated copies of the active 3D model are drawn on a pure black background — one for each face of the pyramid.
04
Reflect
The 45° acrylic faces reflect each panel inward. The reflections converge, creating a floating glowing 3D object in the centre.
03 — Code

The Sketches

Two programs communicate over a USB serial cable. The Arduino sketch is lean — it just watches the sensor and sends commands. The Processing sketch is the brain — it renders all 3D models and responds to those commands.

Arduino — gesture_controller.ino

#include <Wire.h>
#include <SparkFun_APDS9960.h>

SparkFun_APDS9960 apds = SparkFun_APDS9960();
unsigned long lastGestureTime = 0;
const int COOLDOWN_MS = 800;  // ignore gestures for 800ms after one fires

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  if (!apds.init()) { while (1); }  // halt if sensor fails — check wiring
  apds.enableGestureSensor(true);
  Serial.println("READY");  // lets Processing know Arduino is alive
}

void loop() {
  if (apds.isGestureAvailable() && millis() - lastGestureTime > COOLDOWN_MS) {
    lastGestureTime = millis();
    switch (apds.readGesture()) {
      case DIR_LEFT:  Serial.println("L"); break;  // previous model
      case DIR_RIGHT: Serial.println("R"); break;  // next model
      case DIR_UP:    Serial.println("U"); break;  // speed up rotation
      case DIR_DOWN:  Serial.println("D"); break;  // pause / slow down
      case DIR_NEAR:  Serial.println("N"); break;  // zoom in
      case DIR_FAR:   Serial.println("F"); break;  // zoom out
    }
  }
}

Processing — Serial Setup, State & Gesture Handler

import processing.serial.*;

Serial arduino;
String portName = "COM3";  // change to match your Arduino's port

// All animation state in one place — change these to change what you see
int currentModel = 0;
float rotationAngle = 0;
float rotSpeed = 0.015;   // radians per frame
float zoomLevel = 1.0;
boolean paused = false;

void setup() {
  fullScreen();
  background(0);  // pure black background is critical for the illusion
  arduino = new Serial(this, portName, 9600);
  arduino.bufferUntil('\n');
}

void serialEvent(Serial s) {
  String cmd = trim(s.readStringUntil('\n'));
  if (cmd == null) return;
  if      (cmd.equals("R")) currentModel = (currentModel + 1) % 4;
  else if (cmd.equals("L")) currentModel = (currentModel + 3) % 4;  // wraps correctly
  else if (cmd.equals("U")) rotSpeed = min(rotSpeed + 0.01, 0.08);
  else if (cmd.equals("D")) paused = !paused;
  else if (cmd.equals("N")) zoomLevel = min(zoomLevel + 0.2, 2.5);
  else if (cmd.equals("F")) zoomLevel = max(zoomLevel - 0.2, 0.5);
}

Processing — 4-Panel Draw Loop

void draw() {
  background(0);                              // clear to black every frame
  if (!paused) rotationAngle += rotSpeed;     // advance animation unless paused

  // Draw the active model in all 4 pyramid face positions
  drawFace(width/2,   height/4,   PI);        // TOP    — faces up on screen
  drawFace(3*width/4, height/2,   -HALF_PI);  // RIGHT  — faces right
  drawFace(width/2,   3*height/4, 0);         // BOTTOM — faces down
  drawFace(width/4,   height/2,   HALF_PI);   // LEFT   — faces left
}

void drawFace(float x, float y, float extraRotation) {
  pushMatrix();
  translate(x, y);          // move origin to this quadrant's centre
  rotate(extraRotation);    // orient outward toward that pyramid face
  scale(zoomLevel);         // apply zoom
  rotateY(rotationAngle);   // spin the model
  stroke(0, 220, 255);      // iconic Iron Man cyan-blue glow
  strokeWeight(1.5);
  noFill();
  drawModel(currentModel);
  popMatrix();
}

void drawModel(int index) {
  switch(index) {
    case 0: drawArcReactor(); break;
    case 1: drawCrystal();    break;
    case 2: drawSatellite();  break;
    case 3: drawMolecule();   break;
  }
}

04 — Build

Assembly Guide

01
Build the Optical Pyramid
▼

Calculate your trapezoid dimensions from screen size. The formula: top edge = screen width ÷ 6, bottom edge = screen width ÷ 2, height = screen width ÷ 3. For a 10" wide screen that gives 1.7" top, 5" bottom, 3.3" tall. Cut four identical trapezoids from 2mm clear acrylic.

Score the cut line firmly 5–6 times with a craft knife and snap over a table edge — don't try to cut through in one pass. Sand edges lightly with 400-grit sandpaper. Tape together temporarily before gluing to test proportions. The narrow end points down; the wide end faces up and rests on the screen.

Build a black foam board base with a square hole the size of your screen so the pyramid sits centred over it. The base should be at least 2 inches tall to block ambient light from the sides.

Test: Search YouTube for "hologram pyramid video 4K", play it fullscreen, place the pyramid on top, turn off the room lights. Floating glowing object = optics confirmed.

02
Set Up Processing with 4-Panel Display
▼

Download and install Processing 4 from processing.org. Paste in the full Processing code. Temporarily set portName to "null" or comment out the serial lines so you can test visuals without the Arduino connected.

Run the sketch. You should see four synchronised wireframe models on a black background. Place the pyramid on top — the hologram should appear. If it's upside-down, flip the screen 180° or adjust the extraRotation angles in the drawFace() calls.

03
Wire Up Arduino and Sensor
▼

With Arduino unpowered, connect the APDS-9960 following the wiring table. Double-check that VCC goes to 3.3V — the sensor will be damaged at 5V. Install the SparkFun APDS9960 library in Arduino IDE, then upload the sketch. Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud and wave your hand over the sensor — you should see L, R, U, D letters appearing.

Test: Wave left and right 10 times. Reliable L and R outputs = sensor working correctly.

04
Connect Everything Together
▼

Close the Serial Monitor in Arduino IDE before running Processing — only one program can use the serial port at a time. Update portName in your Processing sketch, run it with the pyramid on the screen, and gesture over the sensor. The hologram should respond live.

  • All 4 models load and display correctly
  • Left/right swipes cycle models smoothly
  • Near/far gestures change zoom level
  • Up/down gestures control rotation speed
  • No phantom gestures fire when hand is still
  • Hologram is visible from all 4 sides of the pyramid
05
Polish the Physical Build
▼

Make the Arduino and sensor sit neatly inside or behind the base, with only the sensor's window pointing upward through a small hole near the pyramid. Cable-manage the USB cord so it exits cleanly from the back. Optionally install a strip of blue LEDs inside the base rim — this looks spectacular and improves the illusion's atmosphere dramatically.

05 — Science

How It Really Works

The Pepper's Ghost Illusion

The entire display is built on an optical principle invented in 1862 by physicist John Henry Pepper. When a transparent reflective surface is placed at 45° between a viewer and a hidden light source, the viewer sees a reflection of that source floating in space. Because the reflection appears against a dark background, the brain has no frame of reference to understand it as a reflection — it interprets it as a real, floating, three-dimensional object.

In this build, the hidden light source is the screen facing upward. The four acrylic faces each sit at 45° relative to a viewer on that side and reflect the screen's image. Because all four panels reflect simultaneously, the hologram appears solid from all four sides at once. The critical requirement: the background must be pure black. Any non-black pixel appears as a glow or ghost around the hologram — which is exactly why all Processing code runs on background(0).

Three-Brain Architecture

Brain 1 — Sensor (Arduino + APDS-9960): Translates hand movements into simple text commands over USB serial. Knows nothing about 3D models — purely a translator.

Brain 2 — Renderer (Processing): Maintains 3D model arrays, manages animation state, handles the 4-panel layout, and listens for commands. All the interesting code lives here.

Brain 3 — Optics (the pyramid): Entirely passive — no electronics, no code. Just the laws of physics.

Why Wireframe Rendering

Solid 3D rendering with lighting and shadows is computationally expensive and visually noisy in a hologram context. Wireframe rendering — bright colored lines on pure black — renders in microseconds per frame, maximises contrast for the holographic reflection, and is aesthetically the correct choice. Every sci-fi hologram in film history uses wireframe because it communicates "digital object" to the eye far more powerfully than solid rendering ever could.

Serial Communication

Arduino and laptop talk over USB via UART serial — like two people passing notes. Arduino writes a letter ("R\n") into a buffer; Processing constantly checks that buffer and reads everything up to a newline as a complete command. The 9600 baud rate means 9600 bits per second — more than enough for single-character commands. The golden rule: only one program can use the serial port at a time. Always close Arduino IDE's Serial Monitor before running Processing.

07 — Founder

From the Builder

GaurangFounder, ORB
"

I've always believed that the coolest technology in the world shouldn't be locked behind a Hollywood studio or a billion-dollar lab. When I first saw Iron Man's holographic UI as a kid, I didn't think that's impossible — I thought how do I build that?

ORB started from that exact question. Not as a school project, not as a product — just as my genuine obsession with making the things I imagine actually exist in the real world. I wanted to hold up my hand, wave it, and watch something respond. I wanted the future to feel touchable.

The first time the hologram appeared inside the pyramid and actually reacted to my gesture, I genuinely couldn't stop smiling. That moment — a $45 setup doing something that looks like science fiction — is exactly why I build things.

ORB is just getting started. There are so many ideas I want to bring to life — voice control, live data visualizations, finger tracking — and I'm going to build every single one of them. If you're reading this and you're curious, pick up an Arduino and start. You'll surprise yourself.

— Gaurang
07 — Roadmap

What Comes Next

Easy
Glowing Particle Effects
Orbiting particle trails around each model — each dot follows a circular path offset by a random phase. Dramatic Iron Man feel at near-zero performance cost.
Easy
Scan Line Effect
A bright horizontal stripe that sweeps upward through the hologram — exactly like the Iron Man UI. Just one line() call whose Y position increments each frame and wraps around.
Easy
Color Themes Per Model
Each model gets a signature color — cyan arc reactor, purple crystal, white satellite, green molecule. A simple stroke() change per model in drawModel().
Medium
Model Transition Animations
Instead of snapping instantly between models, animate a dissolve — the old model fades out while the new one fades in with a slight scale-bounce on arrival.
Medium
Raspberry Pi Standalone
Move from a laptop to a Pi 4 running Processing headlessly. Entire system becomes self-contained — power from a USB power bank for fully wireless demos.
Medium
Leap Motion Controller
Replace APDS-9960 with Leap Motion for full finger-tracking — pinch-to-zoom, two-finger rotation, individual finger pointing to interact with the hologram.
Medium
Load Real .OBJ Models
Parse any free .obj file into a vertex/edge array in Processing — display a skull, car engine, or molecular protein as a hologram. Any geometry supported.
Medium
Holographic Dashboard
An always-on ambient display mode showing time, weather, and notifications as glowing icons. Switch between model viewer and dashboard with a long-hold gesture.
Hard
Voice Commands — Jarvis
USB microphone + Python SpeechRecognition to respond to "next model" or "zoom in" — combining voice and gesture for the complete Jarvis experience.
Hard
Live IoT Data Visualization
Connect to a weather API or home sensors and render the data as glowing 3D holographic bar charts or globe projections floating inside the pyramid.
